verses.text: About that time, Judah left his brothers and settled near a man named Hirah, an Adullamite.
There Judah saw the daughter of a Canaanite man named Shua, and he took her as a wife and slept with her.
So she conceived and gave birth to a son, and Judah named him Er.
Again she conceived and gave birth to a son, and she named him Onan.
Then she gave birth to another son and named him Shelah; it was at Chezib that she gave birth to him.
Now Judah acquired a wife for Er, his firstborn, and her name was Tamar.
But Er, Judah's firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the LORD; so the LORD put him to death.
Then Judah said to Onan, "Sleep with your brother's wife. Perform your duty as her brother-in-law and raise up offspring for your brother."

But Onan knew that the offspring would not belong to him; so whenever he would sleep with his brother's wife, he would spill his seed on the ground so that he would not produce offspring for his brother.
What he did was wicked in the sight of the LORD, so He put Onan to death as well.

Then Judah said to his daughter-in-law Tamar, "Live as a widow in your father's house until my son Shelah grows up." For he thought, "He may die too, like his brothers." So Tamar went to live in her father's house.
After a long time Judah's wife, the daughter of Shua, died. When Judah had finished mourning, he and his friend Hirah the Adullamite went up to his sheepshearers at Timnah.
When Tamar was told, "Your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep,"

she removed her widow's garments, covered her face with a veil to disguise herself, and sat at the entrance to Enaim, which is on the way to Timnah. For she saw that although Shelah had grown up, she had not been given to him as a wife.
When Judah saw her, he thought she was a prostitute because she had covered her face.
Not realizing that she was his daughter-in-law, he went over to her and said, "Come now, let me sleep with you." "What will you give me for sleeping with you?" she inquired.
"I will send you a young goat from my flock," Judah answered. But she replied, "Only if you leave me something as a pledge until you send it."
"What pledge should I give you?" he asked. She answered, "Your seal and your cord, and the staff in your hand." So he gave them to her and slept with her, and she became pregnant by him.
Then Tamar got up and departed. And she removed her veil and put on her widow's garments again.
Now when Judah sent his friend Hirah the Adullamite with the young goat to collect the items he had left with the woman, he could not find her.
He asked the men of that place, "Where is the shrine prostitute who was beside the road at Enaim?" "No shrine prostitute has been here," they answered.
So Hirah returned to Judah and said, "I could not find her, and furthermore, the men of that place said, 'No shrine prostitute has been here.'"
"Let her keep the items," Judah replied. "Otherwise we will become a laughingstock. After all, I did send her this young goat, but you could not find her."
About three months later, Judah was told, "Your daughter-in-law Tamar has prostituted herself, and now she is pregnant." "Bring her out!" Judah replied. "Let her be burned to death!"

As she was being brought out, Tamar sent a message to her father-in-law: "I am pregnant by the man to whom these items belong." And she added, "Please examine them. Whose seal and cord and staff are these?"
Judah recognized the items and said, "She is more righteous than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah." And he did not have relations with her again.
When the time came for Tamar to give birth, there were twins in her womb.
And as she was giving birth, one of them put out his hand; so the midwife took a scarlet thread and tied it around his wrist. "This one came out first," she announced.
But when he pulled his hand back and his brother came out, she said, "You have broken out first!" So he was named Perez.
Then his brother came out with the scarlet thread around his wrist, and he was named Zerah.

context.author: Genesis names no author. Jewish and Christian tradition, and the New Testament’s way of speaking of “the Law of Moses” (Luke 24:44), credit the five books of the Law to Moses. Many scholars think Genesis was gathered and shaped from older sources over a long time, and a few remarks look back from a later day: “at that time the Canaanites were in the land” (Genesis 12:6).
context.genre: Family narrative: the story of Joseph and his brothers (Genesis 37 to 50)
context.audience: Israel, the twelve tribes, learning how their fathers came down to Egypt and how God turned evil to good
context.setting: The story leaves Joseph and turns to Judah, who moves away from his brothers, marries a Canaanite woman, and has three sons, Er, Onan and Shelah (vv.1-5). Er marries Tamar but dies, and Onan, told to raise up children for his dead brother, refuses in secret and dies as well (vv.6-10). Judah sends Tamar back to her father’s house to wait for Shelah, “For he thought, ‘He may die too, like his brothers’” (v.11). Years pass and Shelah grows up, but Tamar is not given to him (v.14). When Judah goes up to Timnah for the sheep shearing, she takes off her widow’s clothes, veils herself and sits by the road (vv.12-14). Judah takes her for a prostitute and gives her “Your seal and your cord, and the staff in your hand” as a pledge for a young goat (vv.15-18). When she is found to be pregnant, Judah orders, “Let her be burned to death!” (v.24). She sends him his seal, cord and staff: “I am pregnant by the man to whom these items belong” (v.25). Judah recognizes them and says, “She is more righteous than I” (v.26). Tamar gives birth to twins, Perez and Zerah (vv.27-30).
context.custom: If a man died without a son, his brother was expected to marry the widow and give her a son to carry on the dead man’s name and inheritance; the law of Moses calls this the brother-in-law’s duty (Deuteronomy 25:5-10), and Hittite and Assyrian laws have similar rules. Onan took the marriage but refused the son. A seal worn on a cord was a man’s signature, and a staff often bore its owner’s mark: Tamar holds Judah’s identity in her hands. Sheep shearing was a time of feasting (1 Samuel 25:2-8).
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 39 returns to Joseph in Egypt, in the house of Potiphar.
context.timelineBible: This chapter is set in the middle of Joseph’s story on purpose. Judah, who sold his brother and deceived his father with a goat and a robe, is now deceived with a goat’s price and his own belongings, and he confesses. The changed Judah will offer himself in place of Benjamin (44:33). Perez is an ancestor of David (Ruth 4:18-22), and Tamar is one of four women named in Matthew’s genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:3).

translation.meaning: To do the duty of a husband’s brother: to marry a brother’s widow and raise up a son for him. Levirate marriage takes its name from the Latin levir, brother-in-law.
A pledge or guarantee, held until a debt is paid. The word came into Greek as arrabon, which Paul uses for the Spirit given as a pledge of what is to come (2 Corinthians 1:22).
To be in the right. Judah admits that Tamar was in the right and he was not: she sought what she was owed, and he had withheld it.

gospelParallels.note: Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar.
Perez in the line of Jesus.
The Spirit in our hearts as a pledge.

otBackground.note: May your house become like the house of Perez.

overview.summary: Judah withholds his third son from his widowed daughter-in-law Tamar, so she disguises herself and conceives by Judah; he condemns her until she shows his seal, and he admits she is more righteous than he.
overview.settingLine: Adullam and the road to Timnah, in the hills of Judah.
overview.placeName: Adullam, in the lowland of Judah

history.t: The tribe of Judah, of David and of Jesus, begins in a troubled family.
The twin who broke through first, ancestor of David.

customs.t: A brother married his dead brother’s widow to give her a son.
Marks of a man’s identity and authority.

archaeology.t: Rolled on clay as a signature, often worn on a cord.
Law 193 sets out who marries a dead man’s widow.

overview.discussion: Judah was quick to condemn Tamar until his own seal and staff were put in front of him (vv.24-26). Where am I harsher with others than with myself?
overview.book: The book of Genesis · 50 chapters. Beginnings: creation, the fall, the flood and the nations, then God’s promise to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph.
overview.author: Moses, by tradition

peoplePlaces.d: A widow who claims her right
Twins, ancestors of David and Achan

currentImage.caption: An Old Babylonian cylinder seal (early 2nd millennium BC, Metropolitan Museum of Art). Seals like this were worn on a cord and rolled on clay as a signature. Judah left his “seal and your cord, and the staff in your hand” with Tamar as a pledge (Genesis 38:18).
